en: The Sūtra on the Causes and Conditions of the Youth Prabhāsa, Spoken by the Buddha, Volume One.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master of the Western Heaven, the Court-Attendant Grandee,
Acting Minister of the Court of Imperial Entertainments, and Great Master of the Transmission of the Dharma.
Translated by the Purple-Robed Subject Shi Hu by Imperial Decree. Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at the Kalandaka Bamboo Grove Monastery in the city of Rājagṛha.

Now, in that city, there was an elder named Bhadra, who possessed great wealth, treasures, and sovereign power; yet that elder held deep faith and reverence for the various non-Buddhist practitioners, such as the Nirgranthas.
At one time, due to the causal conditions of that world, the wife of the elder became pregnant.

Then, on a certain day at the time for eating, the World-Honored One, having donned his saffron robes and taken up his alms bowl, entered the city of Rājagṛha to beg for food in sequence, eventually arriving at the residence of the elder Bhadra.
At that time, seeing from afar that the World-Honored One was gradually approaching his house, the elder said to his wife:
"I shall now go with you to the place where the World-Honored One is."
Having spoken these words, he immediately went with his wife to where the Buddha was.
Upon arrival, he addressed him, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
"My name is Sudatta, and this is my wife. She is pregnant and her months are nearly full; as for the one she will give birth to, will it be a boy or a girl?"
The Buddha said, "Householder!

The child in your wife’s womb is certainly a boy. After he is born, your family will flourish and prosper with supreme auspiciousness; appearing among humans, he will enjoy the superior blessings of the devas. Finally, he will go forth from home to study the Path within my Dharma, sever all afflictions, and realize arhatship."
At that time, the elder took a bowl filled with the finest, pure food and offered it to the World-Honored One.
Having accepted it, the World-Honored One spoke these words:
"May the donor be auspicious, peaceful, and happy."
When the World-Honored One had finished speaking, he took the offered food and returned to his original place.

Not long after the Buddha had departed, there was a non-Buddhist practitioner who had previously been held in high esteem by that householder, Subhadra. Upon seeing the Buddha, the World-Honored One, he immediately thought to himself:

"Could it not be that because of this śramaṇa Gautama, the householder has now broken his original faith in me? I ought to go there and inquire about the reason; what does the śramaṇa Gautama come here to preach?"
Then that non-Buddhist, having reflected thus, went immediately to the householder’s residence and spoke these words: “Householder!
What aspiration or request does the śramaṇa Gautama have that he has come to your house?”
"What further did he say?
The householder replied,
"My teacher, the Noble One!"
Because my wife was pregnant, I questioned that śramaṇa Gautama as to whether the child she would give birth to would be a boy or a girl. He said to me:

"She shall certainly give birth to a son; once born, he will surely cause his family to flourish and prosper with supreme auspiciousness. Manifesting among humans, he shall enjoy the superior blessings of the devas, and finally, within my Dharma, he shall leave the household life to study the Path and realize arhatship."

Now, these non-Buddhist practitioners were originally skilled in divination and physiognomy; having heard these words, they immediately took white stones and applied their calculations to determine whether the matter was true or false.
Having performed the calculation, he understood the matter in its entirety; it was exactly as the Buddha had said, truly without any falsehood.
Although that non-Buddhist teacher knew the reality of the situation, he thought to himself:
"If I were now to speak according to the facts, this householder would certainly develop deep faith and respect for the śramaṇa Gautama. I should therefore say this to the householder:"
"Gautama’s teachings contain both truth and falsehood.
Having thought this, that outsider called the elder’s wife to him, took her left and right hands before him, examined the lines on her palms, and scrutinized the features of her face.
At that time, the householder Bhadra addressed the outsider, saying:
"O Noble One, my teacher!
You have already performed the calculation."
"Why do you repeatedly examine the lines on his hands and gaze upon his facial features?
That non-Buddhist replied, "I have just calculated what that Gautama said and examined your wife's physiognomy; I have ascertained the matter, finding it to be partly true and partly false."
The elder spoke again: "Which is real? Which is false?"
The non-Buddhist replied:
"What Gautama has said—that your wife has given birth to a son—is true;
what he said—that once born, the family will become wealthy and prosperous—is also true."

However, at the time of this child's birth, there was a slight sign of fiery radiance; this child will surely destroy your family lineage in the future. As for what was said regarding his supreme auspiciousness and his manifestation among humans to receive celestial blessings—this is false.
"Householder!

Have you not heard that those who receive celestial blessings while in the human world find it difficult to believe? As for what was said regarding those who shall go forth as renunciants within the Dharma of Gautama—this is indeed true. Driven by the pressing necessity of food and clothing, they subsequently resolve to seek the joy of going forth under Gautama."

To say that one has severed all afflictions and realized arhatship is false; for within the Dharma of the śramaṇa Gautama, there is certainly no such thing as severing all afflictions and realizing the fruit of sainthood.
At that time, when the elder Bhadra heard these words—whether they were true or false—his mind was filled with doubt and he became distressed. He then addressed the non-Buddhist teacher, saying:
"O Noble One, my teacher!..."
"What is that matter? What should I now do? The outsider replied:
“Householder, you should cause your son, after he has been born, to go forth and train within my teaching; then he will be able to learn all crafts and activities.
Householder!”
"Although I have spoken thus, you must deliberate for yourself.
Having said this, the non-Buddhist departed from the house.
At that time, the elder Bhadra withdrew to a secluded place and reflected deeply within himself:
"I can no longer cherish anything; I shall cast everything away. I must devise a scheme to destroy the child she carries.
Having thought this, the elder Bhadra took a poisonous drug and rubbed it upon his wife's abdomen.

At that time, as the elder rubbed the medicinal drug on her left side, the fetus shifted to her right; as he rubbed it on her right side, the fetus shifted back to her left. This continued until the entire abdomen was covered, leaving no space to apply more of the poisonous drug. Consequently, his wife immediately met her end.
Sudatta thought to himself:
"Now that my mother has passed away, I too shall follow her in death; thereafter, no one will be left to destroy my family, nor will anyone be able to realize the fruits of the noble path."
At that time, when the elder saw that his wife had already passed away, he immediately wept and wailed aloud.
Neighbors and relatives came to console the Elder Bhadra,
asking, "Why has your wife suddenly died?"
The elder replied, "Because she was pregnant, she suddenly passed away.
After her relatives and neighbors had come to inquire about her, they each returned to their own homes.
The householder Bhadra then reflected to himself:
"My wife has passed away; I should not leave her in the house, but rather provide all necessary items and send her to the Śītavana cemetery."
Having reflected thus, he immediately prepared all the necessary items, intending to go out and deliver them.
His neighbors and relatives, knowing his situation, came again and said to the elder:
"Your wife has already passed away; there is no need to weep, for it will only cause you needless distress."

At that time, the elder took garments of various colors—blue, yellow, red, and white—as well as precious ornaments, and used them to adorn [the body]. The elder then immediately accompanied his kinsmen and relatives in a procession to escort [the body] out and place it in the Śītavana cemetery.

At that time, the non-Buddhist Nirgrantha who had previously performed the divination, having learned of this matter, was filled with great joy; he immediately took up banners and parasols and proceeded forth, magnificently adorned.
In the city of Rājagṛha, throughout the streets, lanes, and crossroads, he addressed the various non-Buddhist followers, such as the Nirgranthas, saying: "Do you know?"
The Śramaṇa Gautama previously said:

"The wife of the householder Bhadra shall give birth to a son; after his birth, the family will become prosperous and most auspicious. Manifesting among humans, he shall enjoy the supreme blessings of the devas, and finally, he shall go forth from home to study the Path within my Dharma, sever all afflictions, and realize arhatship."
"That which you spoke was false. Now the wife of Subhadra has already passed away, and her son has likewise perished.
You should know this: it is like a great tree; once its roots are severed and destroyed, how can its branches, leaves, flowers, and fruits possibly survive?"
When the various non-Buddhist practitioners had finished speaking to one another, their hearts were all filled with joy.

Those who possess pure faith should know that it is the natural law (*dharmatā*) for the World-Honored Buddha to be truly such: there is nothing he does not know, nothing he does not see, nothing he does not understand, and nothing he does not comprehend; having given rise to great compassion, he universally gathers in the world.

He maintains single-minded protective mindfulness and bestows fearlessness; he has already perfected the two practices of śamatha and vipaśyanā, accomplished the three matters of subduing, crossed the great ocean of the four flows of affliction, established himself in the practice of the four bases of psychic power, and universally gathers all sentient beings through the four means of integration.

Throughout the long night, he has constantly contemplated liberation; he has already achieved the four fearlessnesses, severed the five lower fetters, and emerged from the five destinies. He is fully endowed with the six dharmas, and all six pāramitās are perfectly complete. He possesses the six kinds of dharmas constantly practiced by Buddhas, opens the flowers of the seven factors of enlightenment, and realizes the fruit of the eightfold noble path. He has accomplished the samāpattis, perfected the nine preliminary wholesome states, and his ten powers are firm and unshakable. His fame is heard throughout the worlds of the ten directions.

Possessing a thousandfold supreme mastery, three times during the day and three times during the night, he constantly observes the world with the Buddha-eye, turning toward sentient beings with correct knowledge and vision regarding all his activities.
Where is there increase?
Where is there decrease? Where is there affliction?
In what place is there the experience of extreme suffering?
In what place is there destruction?
In what place do such matters as afflictions, extreme suffering, and destruction exist?
In what place is a minor degree of skillful means established?
In what place is the power of great skillful means established?
In what place are the various matters of skillful means established?
In what place do sentient beings fall into the evil realms?
In what place do sentient beings attain birth in the celestial realms?
In what place do sentient beings attain the fruit of liberation?
Where are those sentient beings who have not yet planted roots of goodness?
May they plant roots of goodness.
Where are those sentient beings who have already planted roots of goodness?
He causes them to reach maturity.
As for those sentient beings who have already matured,
he causes them to attain liberation.
The World-Honored Buddha is fully endowed with such merits; his words are without falsehood, and he is free from all faults.

At that time, the World-Honored One, having clearly discerned the time, place, causes, conditions, and other relevant matters, and knowing it was the proper moment to emit light, immediately produced multicolored rays of light—blue, yellow, red, and white—from his mouth. These lights pervaded everywhere, shining brilliantly above and below.

When the light shone downward, all the eight hot hells—the Saṃjīva, Kālasūtra, Saṃghāta, Raurava, Mahāraurava, Tapana, Pratāpana, and Avīci—were completely transformed into coolness once the radiance had illuminated them.

All the Arbuda hells, the Nirarbuda hells, the Aṭaṭa hells, the Hahava hells, the Huhuva hells, the Utpala hells, the Padma hells, and the Mahāpadma hells—these eight cold hells—were entirely transformed into warmth once illuminated by the light, due to the supreme cause of the Buddha’s radiance.
The sentient beings therein, touched by the light, were freed from physical suffering and their minds became joyful; each of them spoke these words:
"By what causal offense have we fallen into this place?"
"Today we behold this rare and wondrous radiance.
When the sentient beings in the hells give rise to such pure minds, the World-Honored One, out of great compassion, further manifests miraculous transformations within the light.
When those sentient beings saw these manifested transformations, they spoke thus:

"Today we have seen these rare and marvelous signs of transformation; having emerged from this place, we shall no longer be reborn in the evil realms. Because of the most supreme causal conditions of the Buddha’s radiance, our bodies are freed from suffering and affliction, and our minds are filled with joy."

Having spoken these words, each gave rise to the most supreme and pure faith; their karmic retributions for the hells were entirely extinguished, and they immediately took birth in the two realms of humans and devas.

The sentient beings in the hells, having received their respective benefits through this reality, were further illuminated by the Buddha’s light as it shone upward upon the Heaven of the Four Great Kings, the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, the Yāma Heaven, the Tuṣita Heaven, the Nirmāṇarati Heaven, the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven, the Brahmakāyika Heaven, the Brahmapurohita Heaven, the Mahābrahmā Heaven, the Parīttābha Heaven, the Apramāṇābha Heaven, the Ābhāsvara Heaven, the Parīttaśubha Heaven, the Apramāṇaśubha Heaven, the Śubhakṛtsna Heaven, the Anabhraka Heaven, the Puṇyaprasava Heaven, the Bṛhatphala Heaven, the Avṛha Heaven, the Atapa Heaven, the Sudṛśa Heaven, the Sudarśana Heaven, and the Akaniṣṭha Heaven.

After the light had thus illuminated these various heavens, it issued from within that radiance the sounds of impermanence, suffering, emptiness, and non-self; furthermore, from within the light, it spoke this verse:

"Just as a great elephant submerged in mud Is able to emerge by means of its courageous strength, So too, through the courageous and mighty power of the Buddha’s teaching, Can the army of birth and death be utterly destroyed."
Now this True Dharma is well-tamed; its practice is far removed from all faults.
It brings rest to the vast cycle of rebirth within the three realms and extinguishes the very limit of sentient beings' suffering.
At that time, the light emitted by the World-Honored One followed its respective paths, pervading the entire trichiliocosm.
Although the Buddha, the World-Honored One, emits but a single ray of light, when it withdraws, its manner varies according to the circumstances:
if the World-Honored One intends to speak of past events, the light immediately vanishes from behind the Buddha.
If he wishes to speak of matters concerning future lives, the light will vanish from before the Buddha;
if he wishes to speak of rebirth in the hells, the light will vanish from the soles of the Buddha’s feet;
if he wishes to speak of rebirth among animals, the light will vanish from the surface of the Buddha’s feet.
If he wishes to speak of matters concerning the realm of hungry ghosts, the light vanishes into the toes of the Buddha’s feet;
if he wishes to speak of matters concerning the human realm, the light vanishes into the Buddha’s knees;
if he wishes to speak of matters concerning a minor wheel-turning king, the light vanishes into the palm of the Buddha’s left hand.
If he wishes to speak of the matters concerning that great universal monarch, the light retracts into the palm of the Buddha’s right hand;
if he wishes to speak of the matters concerning the celestial realms, the light retracts into the Buddha’s navel;
if he wishes to speak of the enlightenment of the śrāvakas, the light retracts into the Buddha’s mouth.
If he intends to speak of the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha, the light will vanish from between the Buddha’s eyebrows;
if he intends to speak of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, the light will vanish from the crown of the Buddha’s head.
Now, the light emitted by the Buddha, the World-Honored One, having shone throughout the trichiliocosm, circled back and vanished into the mouth of the World-Honored One.
At that time, the Venerable Ānanda, who had previously been attending upon the Buddha, saw this radiance and immediately stepped forward with palms joined, addressing the Buddha:
“World-Honored One!

These various wondrous colors and most supreme, pure radiances have issued from the Buddha’s mouth, illuminating extensively and pervading the world. By what causes and conditions has such a thing occurred?”
Having spoken these words, he then recited this verse:
“The Buddha is the most supreme in the world; Abiding in the true cause, he is authentic.
Long ago he distanced himself from dualistic speech, And severed faults such as pride and arrogance.”
Just as a conch shell or a lotus root are naturally white, not due to a lack of cause,
so too the Tathāgata, the most supreme among the honored ones of humanity, manifests radiance, not due to a lack of cause.
By the power of his own conduct and vows, the Tathāgata has realized supernormal powers and great wisdom;
observing that the listeners delight in hearing the Dharma, the Buddha, the Lord of Men, desires to expound it.
The Greatly Wise One, Silent Great Bull King, will surely speak the most supreme and wondrous Dharma;
the Tathāgata proclaims with a single pure voice, severing the net of doubts for all sentient beings.
Furthermore, like the great ocean and the king of mountains, they cannot be moved without a cause.
The Tathāgata, the Perfectly Awakened One, the Honored One among men, does not manifest this mark of radiance without cause.
With great wisdom he observes the workings of causes and conditions; whatever he performs accordingly brings benefit.
Because he accords with the hopes and aspirations of all sentient beings, he manifests such a mark of radiance.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Ānanda, saying: "So it is! So it is!"
Ānanda, you should know that the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha does not emit light without a cause or condition.
I am now about to go to the Śītavana forest; you should go and inform the assembly of bhikṣus, saying:

"The Tathāgata is about to go to the Śītavana forest. You bhikṣus, exert yourselves with diligence and vigor, each donning your saṃghāṭī robes as is appropriate, and attend upon the Tathāgata as he goes to the Śītavana forest."
At that time, Ānanda, having received the Buddha’s instruction, went at once to where the bhikṣus were. Upon arrival, he spoke these words: "The Buddha instructs the bhikṣus:

'The Tathāgata is about to proceed to the Śītavana forest. You bhikṣus, exert yourselves with diligence; each of you should put on your saṃghāṭī robes as is appropriate and attend upon the Tathāgata as we go to the Śītavana forest.'"

At that time, the venerable Ājñātakauṇḍinya, Aśvajit, Vāṣpa, Mahānāman, Bhadrika, Śāriputra, Maudgalyāyana, Kāśyapa, Pūrṇa, and others—this great assembly of śrāvakas—having received the Buddha’s command, immediately donned their saṃghāṭī robes according to the usual custom and came to where the Buddha was.
At that time, the World-Honored One, surrounded by the great assembly before and behind him, proceeded to the Śītavana forest.
That is to say, those who were well-disciplined were surrounded by a host of the disciplined;
those who were liberated were surrounded by a host of the liberated.
The Peaceful One is surrounded by a peaceful assembly;
the One of Discipline is surrounded by an assembly of discipline;
the Worthy One is surrounded by an assembly of those worthy of offerings.
Those free from greed are surrounded by a retinue free from greed;
those with excellent, upright features are surrounded by a retinue with excellent, upright features.
It is just as a bull king is surrounded by a herd of cattle.
Furthermore, he is like a king of elephants surrounded by a herd of elephants;
like a lion king surrounded by various beasts;
like a king of geese surrounded by a flock of geese.
Like the king of the garuḍas, surrounded by a host of garuḍas;
like a brahmin, surrounded by a circle of students;
like a great king of physicians, surrounded by those seeking treatment.
Like a valiant general surrounded by his troops;
like a great wealthy man surrounded by treasures;
like a great caravan leader surrounded by a multitude of merchants.
Like a supreme leader surrounded by a great multitude;
like a minor king surrounded by his ministers and officials;
like a wheel-turning monarch surrounded by a thousand sons.
Like the Moon Deva King surrounded by the multitude of stars;
like the Sun Deva King surrounded by a thousand rays of light;
like Dhṛtarāṣṭra, the Heavenly King of the East, surrounded by the hosts of gandharvas.
Like the Heavenly King Virūḍhaka, surrounded by a host of kumbhāṇḍas;
like the Heavenly King Virūpākṣa, surrounded by a host of nāgas;
like the Heavenly King Vaiśravaṇa, surrounded by a host of yakṣas.
Like the asura king Vemacitrin, surrounded by a host of asuras;
like Śakra, Lord of Devas, surrounded by the host of the Thirty-three Gods;
like the Great Brahmā King, surrounded by the Brahma assembly.
Like a timira fish appearing in the great ocean;
like a massing cloud about to release a great rain, surrounded on all sides by other clouds.

The Tathāgata’s faculties are harmonious, supple, and well-disciplined; his deportment is dignified and solemn, free from any signs of deficiency. Like a great elephant king, his seven limbs rest firmly upon the ground, perfectly level and complete, free from all faults.

The Tathāgata is endowed with the thirty-two major marks and eighty minor characteristics; his sublime adornments and pure physical form are unsurpassed by any. His halo is blazing and radiates vast illumination, like the singular manifestation of light from among a thousand suns.

Furthermore, like a mountain of jewels rising high and prominent, he is the most supreme of all, universally virtuous and excellent, fully endowed with all the qualities of merit such as the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, the three ways in which he needs no protection, the three foundations of mindfulness, and great compassion.
At that time, there were also countless bhikṣus and hundreds of thousands of people who surrounded him on all sides as they followed the Buddha to the Śītavana forest.
When the Buddha travels, there are eighteen qualities that may be praised.
What are these eighteen?
First, he has no fear of fire.
2. No fear of water; 3. No fear of lions; 4. No fear of tigers;
Fifth, there is no fear of perils at sea;
sixth, there is no fear of hostile armies;
seventh, there is no fear of thieves and robbers.
8. No fear of royal troubles; 9. No fear of wicked people;
10. No fear regarding customs duties, ferries, roads, and the like.
11. No fear of humans; 12. No fear of non-humans;
13. No fear of untimely [occurrences];
14. Seeing and hearing with the divine eye and divine ear as they truly are;
15. Manifesting light that shines forth extensively and brilliantly;
16. Attaining mastery over all phenomena.
Seventeenth, mastery over others;
eighteenth, freedom from illness and affliction.
Such virtuous qualities as these were all fully possessed by the Buddha during his travels.

At that time, there were again countless hundreds of thousands of devas and humans who each gathered together and followed the World-Honored One to the Śītavana forest to witness the deeds the Buddha, the World-Honored One, was about to perform.

Translated by the Imperially Commissioned Shi Hu, Prelate of the Court for the Examination of Merit, Great Master of the Transmission of the Dharma, and Recipient of the Purple Robe, by Imperial Decree: At that time, in the city of Rājagṛha, there were two youths;
one was of the Brahmin caste.
They were of the same kṣatriya clan; the kṣatriya boy was named Āyuḥ.
These two boys went out from Rājagṛha and, on the left side of the road, played together.
That youth Āyuṣmān had long since developed right faith, whereas the brahmin youth lacked right faith; he then said to the youth Āyuṣmān:
"I have heard that the World-Honored One previously said:..."

"The wife of the householder Bhadra shall give birth to a son; after his birth, the family shall become prosperous and most auspicious. Manifesting among humans, he shall enjoy the supreme blessings of the devas, until finally, within my Dharma, he shall go forth to study the Path, sever all afflictions, and realize arhatship."
"Since that wife of the noble Sudatta has already passed away, her son must surely have perished with her; the elder’s relatives have sent them to the Śītavana cemetery.
Knowing this to be so, is it not the case that the World-Honored One has spoken a falsehood?"
Then the youth Jīvaka spoke these verses for the sake of the brahmin youth:
"The sun, moon, and stars may fall to the earth; Mountains and rocks may fly from the ground into the sky;
The deep, abyssal waters of the ocean may be made to dry up— But the word of the Buddha is certain and free from falsehood."
At that time, having heard these verses, the young Brahmin said to the youth Āyuṣmat:
"If you do not believe me, I shall now go with you to the Śītavana cemetery to examine this matter for ourselves."
Thereupon, the World-Honored One departed from Rājagṛha and proceeded by stages.
Those two boys were still on the left side of the road, playing together.
At that time, the youth Āyuṣmān, seeing from afar the World-Honored One surrounded by a great assembly, spoke these verses by virtue of his past roots of goodness:
"How marvelous is the Great Muni, Free from all signs of agitation!
The great assemblies of humans and devas Surround him in orderly succession."
With the sound of the lion’s roar, he is able to shatter all external doctrines;
skillfully severing the web of doubts, he is most supreme and difficult to behold.
As the Buddha proceeded to the Śītavana forest, his majestic deportment was worthy of contemplation.
Like dense snow driven by the wind, Cool and refreshing, pervading all space.
O Honored Śākyamuni!
Manifesting transformations of light, Those who behold them for even a moment Obtain benefit according to their needs.
At that time, King Bimbisāra, the ruler of the kingdom of Magadha, heard that the Buddha, the World-Honored One, had previously declared:

"The wife of the elder Bhadra shall give birth to a son; after his birth, his family will become prosperous and most auspicious. He will experience superhuman, celestial blessings in this world, and finally, he will leave the household life to study the Path within my Dharma, sever all afflictions, and realize arhatship."
His wife had already passed away, and the elder’s relatives had carried her body to the Śītavana cemetery.
Now the Buddha, the World-Honored One, surrounded by a great assembly, has also gone to the Śītavana cemetery.
Having heard this, the king immediately reflected to himself:

"If my Buddha, the World-Honored One, were not to go to that Śītavana cemetery for no purpose or benefit, could it be that the wife of Subhadra has died and returned to life, and the World-Honored One intends to go there to perform various acts of benefit for her?"
"I should now go and observe this matter.
Having reflected thus, King Bimbisāra immediately set out, surrounded by elderly ministers, palace ladies, and his official retinue.
When the King was departing the city, those two youths were still on the left side of the road, engaged in play together.
Seeing King Bimbisāra from afar, the youth Jīvaka immediately went forward and spoke these verses:
"The most eminent Lord of Magadha, Surrounded by his ministers and attendants, Is departing from the royal city."
“Having given rise to resolute and pure faith, all the multitudes of people shall rejoice.
At that time, the Buddha, along with the great assembly of devas and humans, King Bimbisāra, and even the youth Āyuṣmanta, all proceeded together to the Śītavana forest.
At that time, the World-Honored One emitted pure light from his mouth, which shone universally upon the assembled multitude.

At that moment, the non-Buddhist Nirgranthas and others who had previously been diviners were also present in the assembly; having seen the Buddha, the World-Honored One, emit this light, they immediately thought:
"Now this Śramaṇa Gautama manifests a sign of light amidst the great assembly; could it be that the son of Subhadra has not yet passed away?"
Having had this thought, he said to the householder: "Householder!
I observe that the śramaṇa Gautama has manifested signs of radiance; surely your son must still be alive and not yet deceased?"
The householder Bhadra replied,
"O Noble One, my teacher! If this is indeed so, what shall I do?"
The non-Buddhist teacher said:
"Householder! If your son survives, you must cause him to enter my teaching and study it thoroughly."

At that time, as the elder was about to cremate his wife, he had already piled up firewood along with her belongings; having placed the corpse in the midst of it, he raised the flames to burn it. Once the fire had broken out, the body suddenly split open gradually from the navel, and from within emerged a lotus flower.
Within that flower sat a youth, sitting upright, with a handsome countenance and extraordinary features.

At that time, the countless multitude in the assembly all beheld this sight and marveled at such an unprecedented occurrence; those of true faith recalled the Buddha’s previous words, realizing they were indeed free from falsehood.
At that time, having observed this matter, the non-Buddhist Nirgrantha felt distress in his heart and remained there in solemn silence.
Then, the World-Honored One addressed the elder Bhadra, saying: "Elder!..."
"You should now take this boy and protect, nurture, and raise him.
At that time, the non-Buddhist Nirgrantha, having secretly observed the features of the elder's face, said: "Elder!..."
"A boy has suddenly emerged from the fire of the cremation pyre; this is inauspicious for all matters, and you should not now take him back to raise him.
At that time, the elder Bhadrika refused to accept him.
At that time, the Buddha said to the youth Āyuṣmān:
"You should take charge of this boy and provide for his protection and upbringing.
Then, after first reflecting carefully, the youth Āyuṣmān addressed the Buddha, saying:
"In my house, there is no place to accommodate him; even if I were to obtain such a son, he would not be suitable for me.
At that time, after the wife of Bhadra had finished burning [the child], the fire extinguished itself through the majestic spiritual power of the Buddha’s radiance.
In an instant, fine snow fell from the heavens, naturally cooling and refreshing; he gathered up the remaining fuel and purified the ground where the fire had burned.
At that time, the boy who had emerged from the flames remained there in perfect composure.
Thereupon, the World-Honored One addressed the youth Āyuṣman and the others, saying:
"You who possess right faith, do not study the heterodox, deceptive, and delusive teachings of outsiders; you should abide in right mindfulness."
The youth Āyuṣman addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

I was born into a royal clan and I have aged within a royal clan. My body is pure, like the exquisite sandalwood from the head of a bull, being exactly the same and no different. I truly do not know of such matters as the deceptive delusions of external paths and heterodoxies.”
At that time, the World-Honored One again addressed the elder Bhadrika, saying:
"This boy is your son; you may take him back home to protect, support, and raise him."
That householder, Subhadra, being firm in his wrong views and not practicing the right path, immediately cast a furtive glance at the face of the non-Buddhist Nirgrantha.
The non-Buddhist practitioners said, "Householder Bhadra!
You should reflect carefully: this boy is a remnant from the midst of fire and is most inauspicious. Although he was not burned by the flames, how could his physical marks possibly be auspicious?"

If you take him back, it will certainly cause the destruction of your family; furthermore, it will not be beneficial for your life, will bring much suffering and affliction upon your person, and whatever you desire will not be fulfilled.
"Reflect deeply upon this for yourself; it would not be right to regret it later.
Having heard the words of the non-Buddhist ascetics, the elder still refused to accept them.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed King Bimbisāra, saying:
“Great King! You should now take this boy and raise him within the royal palace.

At that time, King Bimbisāra, having received the Buddha’s instruction, immediately rose from his seat, bowed with his body bent, and reached out his hand to take the boy. Having gazed upon him from all sides, he addressed the Buddha, saying:
"I have brought this child back to the royal palace in accordance with the Buddha's command.
However, what name shall this boy be given?
I pray that the Blessed One, the World-Honored One, will graciously establish one for him."
The Buddha said, "Great King!
Since this boy was obtained from within the fire, you should establish a name for him and call him 'Fire Radiance' (Jyotirprabha)."
At that time, the World-Honored One, having entrusted this youth to King Bimbisāra in the midst of the great assembly,

immediately observed and thoroughly understood King Bimbisāra and the entire congregation— their physical constitutions, their natures, and the inclinations of their minds— and accordingly preached the Dharma extensively for them as was appropriate.

When this assembly had heard the Dharma, many hundreds among them gave rise to the most supreme, pure, and correct faith; some realized the fruit of *srotāpanna*, some realized the fruit of *sakṛdāgāmin*, some realized the fruit of *anāgāmin*, and some realized the fruit of *arhat*. Some were able to advance and give rise to the roots of goodness of the stage of *ūṣmagata*; some were able to advance and give rise to the roots of goodness of the stage of *mūrdhan*; some were able to advance and give rise to the roots of goodness of the stage of *kṣānti*. Some gave rise to the mind of *śrāvaka-bodhi*, some gave rise to the mind of *pratyekabuddha-bodhi*, and some gave rise to the mind of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. Some gave rise to the mind of taking refuge and seeking protection, and some gave rise to the mind of upholding the precepts (*śikṣāpada*).

Thus, by the power of the Buddha’s merit and the power of the True Dharma, as well as through the assembly’s harmonious cooperation, all members of the gathering obtained benefit according to their respective needs.
At that time, King Bimbisāra departed from the Buddha’s assembly and took this boy back to the royal palace.
At that time, the Great King summoned eight palace ladies to serve as his eight mothers:
two were appointed as foster mothers to provide loving care,
and two were appointed as wet nurses to provide suckling.
Two were appointed as cleansing mothers to bathe and wash him;
two were appointed as play-mothers to accompany him in his games and pastimes.

Thus the King commanded these eight mothers to take charge of the boy, from the time he was nursed at the breast until he reached maturity, providing him with milk, food, and whatever else was required.
Throughout day and night, he nurtured and raised him with compassionate care, ensuring that nothing was lacking.
Later, as the child gradually grew up, he was like a single lotus emerging in full splendor from a pure pond; the manner in which he was cherished, protected, and treasured was likewise.
Later on, the youth Prabhāsa had an uncle who had long held wealth and set out for trade abroad; as the years gradually passed, he was unable to return.
Suddenly, at one time, he heard people outside say:
"My sister is pregnant; the Buddha has prophesied for her:

'She will certainly give birth to a son. After his birth, the family will become wealthy and prosperous, most excellent and auspicious. Manifesting among humans, he shall enjoy the supreme blessings of the devas, and finally, within my Dharma, he will leave the household life to study the Path, sever all afflictions, and realize arhatship.'"
When his uncle heard these words, he immediately and swiftly gathered the merchant’s goods, carried them over a long distance, and returned to his own home.
Having arrived at her home, she learned that her sister had already passed away; she wailed and wept piteously, reflecting deeply within herself:
"Previously, when I was outside, I heard the Buddha’s prophecy that my sister would certainly give birth to a son, and would eventually sever all afflictions and realize arhatship."
"Now that my sister has already passed away, the Buddha’s words were spoken in vain; could it be that even the World-Honored Buddha speaks falsely?
Having had this thought, she immediately went to a neighbor's house to inquire about the matter, saying to the neighbor:
"I have just returned from abroad after traveling for trade. Previously, I heard people say that my sister was pregnant, and the Buddha made a prediction regarding her."

"You shall certainly give birth to a son; after his birth, the family will flourish and attain supreme auspiciousness. While among humans, he will enjoy the superior blessings of a deva, and finally, within my Dharma, he will leave the household life to study the Path, sever all afflictions, and realize arhatship."
Having heard these words, I returned home with joy.
However, upon arriving at my house, I found that my younger sister had already passed away. Could what the Buddha said not be false?
At that time, a neighbor spoke to his maternal uncle, reciting a verse:
"The stars and moon may fall to the earth, Mountains and rocks may fly into the sky,
The great ocean may be made to dry up— But the Buddha’s word is truly without falsehood."
When that neighbor had finished speaking these verses, he further said to his maternal uncle:
"What the World-Honored One has spoken is truly without falsehood; although your sister has passed away, there is indeed a cause for it."

Because the householder Bhadraśobhana, having placed his faith in the words of non-Buddhist heretics, committed the act of killing, your sister passed away due to those causal conditions of slaughter. However, the youth Prabhāsa possesses great majestic power; fire could not burn him, and he emerged from within a lotus flower, where he is now being raised in the palace of King Bimbisāra.
At that time, the neighbor reported the preceding events in detail to his maternal uncle.
Upon hearing these words, the uncle immediately returned home and said to the elder Suvīra:
"The actions you have taken, Elder, do not accord with the principles of Dharma. For what reason has my sister met her end?"
However, I know for certain that my sister was pregnant; you devised a scheme to prevent her from giving birth safely.
Driven by false views and having placed your faith in non-Buddhist paths, you created the conditions for murder and killed my sister.
The youth Prabhāsa possesses great power; fire cannot burn him, as he emerged from within a lotus flower. He is currently in the royal palace, which is truly improper.
You should go quickly to the royal palace this very day and bring the youth back; that would be most excellent.

"If it is not so, I shall certainly cause discord between you and him; I will take white lime and scatter it everywhere throughout the streets, lanes, crossroads, and all other places, making the ground entirely white and causing people to be struck with wonder."
I shall proclaim:
"The householder Bhadra has murdered a woman; my sister previously lost her life because of this man.
Now that the youth Prabhāsa is in the royal palace, the King likewise acts without benefit at this time."
"Wherever I may go, I shall certainly say this; you must deliberate for yourself so as not to bring shame upon yourselves later.
At that time, having heard these words, the elder Bhadra felt distress in his heart and thought to himself:
"Is what my maternal uncle says not indeed the truth?"
"If it be truly so, I shall surely be filled with shame.
Having reflected thus, he immediately went to the royal palace.
Upon arriving at the king's presence, he prostrated himself in reverence and reported the preceding events in detail to the king, saying:

“Great King! I am still young and insignificant, whereas Your Majesty is most supreme and eminent. If you do not grant this boy to me, I fear it will bring reproach upon Your Majesty; I pray that Your Majesty grant this boy to me now.”
The King said: "Householder!
It was not with my own intention that I took this boy; it was the Buddha, the World-Honored One, who entrusted him to me. Had it not been by the Buddha’s command, how could I have taken him?"
"If you wish to take this boy, you should now go in person to the Buddha's presence and state your intention in detail.
At that time, the elder Bhadra immediately left the royal palace and went to where the Buddha was.
Having arrived, he addressed the Buddha, saying:
"I have relatives who have returned from abroad. They said to me:
'The Youth Prabhāsa is currently in the royal palace; it would be most excellent if you could have him brought back this very day.'"
If it were not so, they would not have been reconciled; furthermore, he shall go to a crossroads and proclaim:
"The noble man has murdered a woman; my sister’s life was taken by this very person."
"The youth Prabhāsa is currently in the royal palace, and the king is likewise acting without benefit at this very moment.
Thinking thus, I went straight to the royal palace to seize that youth.
The king said:
"Previously, it was because the Buddha commanded that he be taken in and raised.
Therefore, I have come here; I pray that the Buddha will cause the king to return this boy to me."

At that time, the World-Honored One, having understood this matter, observed that if the householder Bhadra were not to obtain this boy now, there would be no possibility that his heart would not be overwhelmed by suffering; he would certainly vomit blood and meet his end.
The Buddha, out of great compassion, acted as their protector and said to the Venerable Ānanda: "Ānanda,
you should go to the palace of King Bimbisāra and speak these words on my behalf:"
“The Buddha asks the Great King if you are free from illness.
Now there is a matter regarding which you should listen to the Buddha’s words:
‘The householder Bhadra has come to take the youth Prabhāsa; Your Majesty should now promptly grant him to him.’”
If the householder Bhadra were not to obtain this boy, it would be impossible for his heart not to be oppressed by suffering; he will certainly vomit blood and meet his end.
"The King should attend to all these matters exactly as the Buddha has spoken.
At that time, the Venerable Ānanda, receiving the Buddha’s holy command, immediately went to the palace of King Bimbisāra. Upon arrival, he saw the King and spoke to him in the words of the Buddha:
"The Buddha asks the Great King: Are you free from illness?"
Now there is a matter regarding which you should listen to the Buddha’s words:

The elder Bhadra has come to take the youth Prabhāsa. If Bhadra does not obtain this youth, it is impossible that his heart will not be overwhelmed by anguish; he will certainly vomit blood and meet his end.
"Great King, you should be fully aware of these matters;
it is fitting that you grant them [the kingdom] immediately. At that time, King Bimbisāra, having received the Buddha’s command, spoke these words:
"Virtuous Honored One!..."
Returning to the place where the Buddha was, he made this request to convey my words:

"King Bimbisāra bows his head at the feet of the World-Honored One and pays his respects, inquiring after the World-Honored One’s well-being; as the Buddha has instructed, I have already received and accepted those teachings."
At that time, the Venerable Ānanda immediately left the royal palace, returned to where the Buddha was, and reported everything the king had said to the World-Honored One.
Then King Bimbisāra quickly summoned the elder Subhadra; once he had arrived, the king said to him: "Subhadra!"

This youth has long resided within the palace, where he was protected, nurtured, and attended by eight nurses; his nursing and feeding were provided according to the proper seasons, and I have cherished him with an affection that exceeds even that for my own son.
Although I have now returned this to you by the Buddha’s command, you should also understand my intention: come each day at the three times of the day and bring it yourself, for I wish to behold it.
The householder Bhadra respectfully accepted the king’s command and addressed the king, saying:
“Having received Your Majesty’s decree, how could I dare not comply? I shall go to Your Majesty’s presence three times every day.”

At that time, King Bimbisāra immediately adorned a great elephant with various precious and exquisite ornaments, had the youth Prabhāsa mount this jeweled elephant, and separately commanded his ministers and officials to escort him to the house of the elder.

Thereafter, the elder went to the royal palace three times every day to present the Youth Prabhāsa to the king, who personally observed that all the actions performed by the youth were entirely in accordance with the Dharma.

In time, when his father, the virtuous Bhadra, had passed away, the youth Prabhāsa became the head of the household. Having inherited the family estate, he redoubled his diligence, placing faith in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha of bhikṣus; he took refuge in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha of bhikṣus.
The father of that man, the householder Bhadra, had previously committed an act of killing in this very place;

the householder Prabhāsa is now performing meritorious deeds on his behalf, constantly providing within his own home the four requisites in abundance to serve and support the bhikṣus from the four quarters, even those who will later compile the Blessed One’s treasury of the True Dharma.
The foremost elders and all the great śrāvakas were also constantly provided with their necessities and offerings.
In the city of Rājagṛha, the elder Ghoṣila performed various such meritorious deeds, all for the benefit of his father.

At that time, there was a merchant who had previously been a fellow trader with the elder Sudatta; they were old companions who had long been abroad on business and had not yet returned. This man had always thought that Sudatta did not perform virtuous deeds, and he further learned that the elder had now passed away, leaving a son named Prabhasa to succeed him as the head of the household.
The elder Prabhāsa had faith in the Buddha, faith in the Dharma, and faith in the Saṅgha of bhikṣus; he had taken refuge in the Triple Gem and acted in accordance with the Dharma.

When the merchant heard of these matters, he felt sorrow for Sukhīti and rejoiced in the elder Prabhāsa. He immediately fashioned a large alms bowl from exquisite gośīrṣa sandalwood, filled it with various jewels, and sent a messenger from a distant foreign land to bring it as a token of goodwill to the elder Prabhāsa.
Furthermore, he instructed the messenger to convey these words:
"May what has been requested be remembered for a long time and never forgotten.
At that time, the Elder Prabhāsa empowered it with a mantra, which is as follows:
“Ke na cchi ha ṭya va (1) | Śṭha ṭya va (2) | Kā ri ka ṭa ke na va (3) | Gṛ he ḍma (4). Having spoken this mantra, he further said:
“If a śramaṇa, a brāhmaṇa, or one of great power and supernormal faculties should receive this precious bowl, they shall obtain happiness as is appropriate.”

Having performed this empowerment, he took the bowl and departed from Rājagṛha. First, on the left side of the road, he erected a great pillar, adorned and decorated with colorful paintings, with a bell suspended above it; he placed the bowl beneath it to serve as a permanent marker.

At that time, there were various non-Buddhist practitioners who, according to their customary practice, went to the river at dawn to bathe. Passing by along the way, they saw this precious bowl and immediately asked the elder Prabhāsa: "Elder!..."
"You have placed this bowl here; what is it for?
The householder Prabhāsa related the original circumstances in detail to the non-Buddhists.
Those non-Buddhists said:
"Only those pure śramaṇas, sons of the Śākya, are worthy to receive this bowl; others lack the power and capacity to receive it.
Having spoken thus, the non-Buddhists dispersed to their respective places.

Subsequently, there were elder and venerable bhikṣus who entered the city of Rājagṛha to beg for alms with their bowls. They too saw this precious bowl on the left side of the road and asked the Elder Prabhāsa:
"For what purpose have you placed this bowl here?"
The householder Prabhāsa also gave his detailed answer based on the original cause,
just as he had done before. The bhikṣus said, "Householder!"
"This precious bowl is not for us to receive; it should be offered to the Buddha, for this will increase our virtuous benefits and extinguish all defilements of sin.
When the bhikṣus had spoken thus, they dispersed to their respective places.
