Translated by the Imperial Edict by the Subject Shi Hu, the Grand Master of the Transmission of the Dharma and former Minister of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices, who has been granted the purple robe: At that time, the Venerable Daśabala-Kāśyapa, while traveling, arrived at the place where the precious bowl had been set down. Having witnessed this event, he went immediately to the house of the elder Prabhāsa and asked him:
"Why have you placed this precious bowl on the left side of the road? What is its intended use?"
The householder Prabhāsa then related the preceding circumstances in detail to the Venerable One.
At that time, Daśabala Kāśyapa thought to himself:

“I have heard that the householder Bhadra placed his faith in non-Buddhist paths and previously committed an act of killing; yet now the householder Prabhāsa is performing meritorious deeds in this very place. I ought not to depart with this bowl, but should instead manifest my supernormal powers to fulfill the aspirations of the householder Prabhāsa.”
Having reflected thus, he immediately employed his supernormal power; like a strong man extending or contracting his arm, he took the precious bowl and returned to his dwelling with it.
At that time, when the bhikṣus saw Daśabala Kāśyapa approaching carrying a precious bowl, they all spoke to him together, saying:
"Venerable One! From where did you obtain this bowl?"
Daśabala Kāśyapa related the preceding events in full to the bhikṣus.
Then the bhikṣus addressed him again, saying:
"Venerable One!"
“Did you manifest such supernatural power for the sake of this bowl in accordance with the proper ritual?
Daśabala Kāśyapa replied, “O Bhikṣus!”
Was it performed according to the ritual protocol? Or was it not performed according to the ritual protocol?
I have already completed the act; what can be done now?
Then the bhikṣus reported the matter in its entirety to the Buddha.
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus, saying:

"If it is at an improper time or place, or if it serves no purpose or benefit, one should not suddenly manifest supernatural powers or similar signs. What is manifested in such an unsuitable manner will inevitably give rise to faults."
At that time, the World-Honored One, by means of his supernormal powers, manifested four bowls:
the first of gold,
the second of silver;
Third, vaidūrya; fourth, sphaṭika.
Having manifested these four, he further manifested four alms bowls:
First, brass; second, red copper;
third, white copper.

4. Wood. Having thus performed these transformations, he arranged the first four bowls in sequence and likewise arranged the latter four bowls. Within each bowl, he filled them to the brim with excellent, edible medicinal incense and placed them all in one location, instructing the community of bhikṣus that those who were permitted to receive them might take as they pleased.
Thereafter, the Buddha withdrew his supernormal power, and the bowl no longer appeared.

Subsequently, from time to time, there spontaneously manifested signs of supreme merit, auspicious omens, and extraordinary occurrences belonging to the householder Āloka, who was preeminent among the gods.
At that time, between the two realms of Rājagṛha and Campā, there was a boundary pillar adorned with colorful paintings;
beneath it were two bowls: one of iron and one of clay.
Having first empowered this bowl, he placed it here within these two realms.
Not far away was a customs station where various merchants paid their dues to the king.

There was once a tax collector who, though possessed of many sons, kinsmen, and abundant wealth, did not cultivate merit. He suddenly passed away while at his place of taxation and became a great evil yakṣa, remaining in that very region to guard the tax station.
One night, the sons all dreamed that a yakṣa said to them:

"You should place a large bell upon a pillar marking that ground. Whenever any merchants pass through this customs station, if they have taxable goods hidden and fail to pay duty, the bell will move of its own accord."
The tax collectors, having learned of this, immediately and swiftly assembled their men to search again; once they had recovered the taxed goods, they allowed them to depart.
When the sons received the dream, at dawn the next morning, they went with their kinsmen to the side of the toll station, found the pillar, and according to the dream, hung the bells upon it.
At that time, in the kingdom of Campā, there was a householder Brahmin named Manthānamuṇḍa who made his living through trade.
Once, while he was in one place together with his wife, the wife said to her husband:
"I have been managing the household affairs with you, increasing our wealth and grain to provide for our needs; how can you remain so complacent as to do nothing at all?"

"You should now go to the marketplace and purchase the finest, most exquisite cotton flower-petals; I shall weave them for you into white cotton cloth, which you can then take out and trade. Will there not be profit?"

Then the brahmin, acting according to his wife’s words, purchased it and brought it home. His wife then set out the loom and its implements, arranging them in order, and began weaving the cotton cloth (*karpāsa*). It was fine and soft, of incomparable excellence; she wove it with warp and weft so that it was dense, fine, and even.

Having woven this cloth with such diligent effort, she said to her husband: "This white cloth is of the highest quality, fine and soft, worth a thousand pieces of gold. You may take it outside; if someone offers the price of a thousand pieces of gold, you should give it to them."

If its price is less than a thousand pieces of gold, you should go from place to place and utter these light words: "In this place there is no one capable of discerning this exquisite, fine cotton cloth."
Having spoken these words, he immediately took it and went elsewhere to trade.

At that time, the Brahmin Manṛtamo, following his wife’s instructions, took this fine cotton cloth to the market to trade, yet in the end, no one offered even a thousand pieces of gold in exchange for it.
Recalling what his wife had said, he exclaimed:
"In the great city of Campā, there is not a single person who recognizes this fine cotton cloth.

Having said this, he took it home and consulted with his wife: "Since no one here will pay the price for this, we should go to another country; surely there must be someone who recognizes it. After they had thus informed each other, [he set out].

Then the brahmin took another piece of cloth he had previously worn and, together with the new cotton cloth as before, placed it inside the handle of his umbrella; accompanied by the group of merchants, he traveled on while concealing it, gradually departing from his own country.

He traveled toward Rājagṛha, passing through all the tax stations within those two territories; once the merchants arrived there, they set down their随行 goods (articles carried along) and gathered them together in one place.
At that time, the tax collectors searched through the goods in order. Each of the merchants then delivered their respective taxable items to the king.
Among the crowd, there was only the Brahmin Manṛtamo, who concealed the white cotton cloth he had previously placed inside his staff and failed to deliver it, remaining alone to one side.
At that time, the bell attached to the pillar previously erected as a marker beside the toll station spontaneously began to ring.
The tax collector, realizing immediately that there was someone among the multitude concealing taxable goods, said to the caravan leader:

"Now this bell upon the pillar has sounded of its own accord; it was neither moved by the wind nor struck by anyone. I have discerned clearly that within this group of yours, is there not someone who has concealed taxable items and failed to pay the duty?"

Thereupon, the tax collector immediately summoned them in haste and searched them once more; yet among this multitude, he did not see a single person who possessed taxable goods that they had concealed and failed to pay.
At that time, the merchants, having mutually confirmed that there were no goods subject to taxation, all desired to proceed; yet the bell rang once more.
This occurred three or four times in succession, and after repeated and meticulous inspections, it was found that there was no one concealing taxable goods.

The merchant leader then said to the tax collector, "There is no one among this group of mine who has concealed any goods for duty; it must have been someone from another group who departed privately.
Having spoken thus, the assembly deliberated together and concluded that it was this particular brahmin who had hidden the taxable goods.
Finally, that tax collector seized the Brahmin Manthāṭamu and would not let him go, persistently demanding his tax.
At that time, the Brahmin said:
"For what reason do you now conspire to seize me?"
"You have already demonstrated that I truly possess nothing; if there were even the slightest thing hidden that you did not accept, I would exhaust all that I own and offer it all as tax.
Having said these words, the bell rang once more.
At that time, the tax collector thoroughly searched this brahmin’s place and said to him: "Hey! Brahmin!"
"For what reason do you now stubbornly conceal these goods and refuse to pay the tax?

You have heard this bell sound vibrating repeatedly; such a thing is rare. You should know that beneath this pillar there must be a celestial deity providing protection. You ought to deliver the goods so as not to bring blame upon yourself."
The Brahmin said, "By the power of the devas, I believe this to be true. Having spoken,
he drew a white woolen cloth from within the handle of his parasol and showed it to the tax collector, saying these words:
"This is my evaded tax; you should take it. When the tax collector had received the cotton cloth, he said to the brahmin, "Since you have not paid it to the king, I shall not accept it;
I shall instead offer it to the celestial deity."
Having spoken thus, he took the cotton cloth and hung it upon a pillar, then said to the brahmin:
"I have already hung this cloth as an offering to that celestial deity; if you so desire, you may take it yourself."

Then the brahmin took the cotton cloth and proceeded forward; at a secluded spot, he again placed it inside the handle of his umbrella as before, concealing it as he walked, and gradually entered the city of Rājagṛha.
At that time, the brahmin spread out his cotton cloth and displayed it for sale in the marketplace, hoping that someone would pay the price of one thousand pieces of gold;
he traveled about in this manner until, in the end, no one offered the price of one thousand pieces of gold.
At that time, the brahmin proclaimed:
"In the great city of Rājagṛha, there is no one capable of identifying this exquisite, fine cotton cloth.
As he spoke these words, the Elder Prabhāsa was riding upon a precious elephant, returning from the royal palace to his own residence.
Upon hearing these words, he was suddenly struck with alarm and astonishment; he stopped immediately for a moment and said to the Brahmin:
"For what reason do you now utter such disparaging words here in this city?"
That brahmin immediately had no reply. The elder Prabhāsa said,
"You should fully explain the original cause of this matter."

The brahmin said, "I have come from my own country bringing these two pieces of exquisite, fine cotton cloth for trade. If anyone were to offer me a price of one thousand gold pieces, I would give them to him; yet I have traveled everywhere, and no one has offered such a price."
The householder Prabhāsa said, "Bring it here; I shall examine it for a moment.
Thereupon, the brahmin followed the householder into his residence, where he spread out the cotton cloth and showed it to him.
Having seen them, the householder was able to distinguish them immediately and said to the brahmin:
"Of these two pieces of cotton cloth, one is new and one is old; for the old one, I shall give you five hundred gold coins."
The brahmin said, "The price offered by the elder is not appropriate.
The elder Prabhāsa replied:
"I see clearly now that this is an old cloth; it has become new only after being washed.
The householder immediately took this old cotton cloth and threw it from the air down from the upper story of the multi-storied pavilion. Because the cloth was heavy, it fell rapidly to the ground.
The householder Prabhāsa further said to the brahmin,
"I wish to examine another new piece of cotton cloth. Thereupon,
the brahmin immediately took the new cotton cloth and presented it to the householder.
Having observed this, the elder, as before, threw it toward the sky; because the body of the fine woolen cloth was light, it took a long while to slowly descend to the ground.
That Brahmin immediately conceived deep faith and respect, and spoke these words:
"The Elder Prabhāsa possesses great majestic power. Whether this fine woolen cloth be new or old, I offer it all to you without taking any payment; you should accept it."
The householder replied, "My family is immensely wealthy, and you have endured great hardships; how could I accept these goods from you without a name?
I shall now give you one thousand gold coins each; sell me these two pieces of cotton cloth."
When the brahmin had received the price, he took it back to his residence.
The Elder Prabhāsa first gave the old cotton cloth to his domestic servant, and later, taking the new cotton cloth, he made it into a pure towel for his own regular use.
Later, when the householder Prabhāsa had finished using this towel, he hung it out to dry in the sun.

At that moment, King Bimbisāra, surrounded by his ministers and officials, was about to ascend the palace terrace when a sudden violent wind blew the bathing towel away, causing it to fall before the king.
At that time, King Bimbisāra said to his attendants:
"From where does this fine cotton cloth come?
Only one who is a king ought to enjoy its use."
The attendant ministers said:

"Great King, have you not heard that when a Wheel-Turning Sage King ascends the throne, the heavens rain down gold for seven days? Now that Your Majesty presides over the realm, the heavens rain down fine cotton cloth; it will surely not be long before they also rain down gold."
The king said, "Do you know?

I have heard the Buddha’s prophecy that the Elder Prabhāsa will manifest among humans and receive the supreme blessings of the devas. This fine cotton cloth must surely be his possession, which has been blown here by the wind; you should summon that man and return it to him."
At that time, the householder Prabhāsa went before the king, and the king said: "Householder!
The Buddha previously prophesied for you that you would now receive supreme celestial blessings among human beings. This fine cotton cloth must surely be yours; I now return it to you."
Then, the householder Prabhāsa bowed deeply and reached out his hand to receive the cotton cloth. Having received it and examined it, he saw that it was his own;
he then addressed the king, saying: "This is the clean towel used in my home. It happened that while it was being dried in the sun, the wind blew it here. This is exactly how it occurred."
The King said: "Householder!
The Buddha has prophesied for you that you shall receive supreme heavenly blessings; auspicious signs have appeared, and the Buddha’s words are true and sincere—such indeed is the matter."
He further said: "Householder!
Since your auspicious marks are now such as these, why do you not invite the King to your residence for a brief visit?"
The householder said,
"I pray that Your Majesty will deign to visit my humble abode this very day.
The king replied:
“Householder! You may first return and prepare various foods and drinks.
The householder replied:
“Great King! Those who enjoy celestial blessings do not need to labor at construction; it is spontaneously accomplished. We pray that Your Majesty will deign to visit.
Thereupon, King Bimbisāra, surrounded by his ministers and attendants, went forth to the house of the elder Prabhāsa.

Led by the elder, the king arrived at his house; at the outer gate, he saw a female gatekeeper whose physical appearance was extraordinary, so the king paused for a moment. The elder addressed him, saying:
"Great King, for what reason do you stop and not proceed?"
The king said, "Householder!
It was because I saw your wife that I paused for a moment."
The householder replied, "This is not my wife; she is a door-keeping maidservant.
The king then proceeded forward to the middle gate, where he again saw a door-keeping maidservant. The king still did not advance, and the householder spoke again.
"For what reason does the King remain stationary and not proceed?
The King answered as before.
The householder said:
"This is not my wife; she is merely a maidservant guarding the middle gate.

The king then proceeded forward and entered the middle gate. Seeing upon the ground of mani-jewels the patterns of insects, fish, and flowing water, the king thought it was a pond and paused there for a moment.
The elder said, "Great King,
for what reason do you remain here and not proceed?
The king replied:
"There is water here, therefore we do not proceed forward.
The elder addressed him, saying: "Great King!"
"There is no water here; this ground is composed of mani jewels.
The king said, "Householder!"
"If this is a ground of jewels, why are there such signs as various insects, fish, flowing water,
and so forth? The elder replied, "Great King!"
"Above, there are revolving wheels carved with the forms of insects, fish, and other creatures; below, it is thus because it is illuminated by the light of *maṇi* jewels.

Although the king heard this explanation, he still did not believe it. He immediately took his own signet ring, threw it forward onto the ground, and as the ring struck the earth, its sound caused the king to finally believe that the ground was made of *maṇi* jewels.
When King Bimbisāra had entered the house and taken his place upon the lion throne,
the elder’s wife came forth to prostrate before the king, and suddenly tears fell from her eyes.
The king said,
"Householder! Why does your wife shed tears upon seeing the king?"
The elder addressed him, saying:
"Great King! Your wife bows before you; how could she dare shed tears?"
It is simply because the garments worn by Your Majesty have the scent of wood smoke, and as that smoke irritates the eyes, tears suddenly fall.
Therefore, Great King!
For one who enjoys celestial blessings, whatever food or drink is desired, there is a wish-fulfilling gem (*cintāmaṇi*) from which it naturally emerges.
At that time, King Bimbisāra was staying at the house of the elder for seven days and forgot to return to the royal palace.
Then the ministers and officials went together to Prince Ajātaśatru and said to him: "Prince!..."

The King has been at the house of the Elder Prabhāsa for seven days now; his state affairs have been hindered and neglected. It is fitting that the Crown Prince go and request the King to return to the palace.
At that time, Prince Ajātaśatru went to the house of the elder Prabhāsa and said to his father the king, "My King,
for what reason have you forgotten to return to the royal palace?"
"In matters of state administration, there will be hindrances and neglect.
The King said, "I have been in this residence for only a single day; when there are affairs of state in the kingdom, can you not temporarily act on my behalf to govern?"
The Prince addressed him, saying:
"Father King, you should know that we have been staying in this house for seven days already.
When the King heard these words, he looked toward the Elder Prabhāsa and asked:
"Is it truly so?
The householder replied,
"It is indeed so, Great King!"
"It has already been seven days.
The King said, "Householder!"
"In this house of yours, by observing what sign do you distinguish day from night?
The householder replied,
"By the opening and closing of the flowers, we distinguish day from night."
The distinction between day and night is made by the harmonious and discordant songs of various birds;
the distinction between day and night is also made by the appearance and disappearance of the light of mani jewels.
Furthermore, there are flowers that close though it is not night, and flowers that bloom though it is not day.
There is the light of the jewel manifest though it is not night; there is the light of the jewel hidden though it is not day.
There are exotic birds silent though it is not night; there are exotic birds singing in harmony though it is not day.
At that time, having heard these words, King Bimbisāra immediately said to the householder Prabhāsa:
"I believe the Buddha’s words; they are true and not false."
"What the Buddha has said—that you are currently receiving supreme celestial blessings among humans—is indeed true.
Having spoken these words, King Bimbisāra departed from the householder's residence.

When Prince Ajātaśatru was about to depart from his residence, he secretly took a maṇi jewel named Śaṅkhakuṭa and gave it to an attendant. Having returned to the royal palace, he summoned him and said:
"The maṇi jewel you were given just now—you must bring it here; I wish to examine it."
The attendant opened his hand, intending to present it to the Prince, but the pearl was not there;
he immediately said, "I do not know where this pearl has been lost."
At that time, the Prince immediately took his attendant and began to beat him.
By the power of his celestial merit, the Elder Ghoṣadatta immediately became aware of this matter and came to ask the Prince:
"For what reason are you beating this attendant?"
The Prince replied:
"I went to your house and stole the maṇi jewel, which I gave to this attendant; now you suddenly conceal it.
I have already committed a theft, and you have committed a further theft by stealing from me; since your offense is even more grave, I am therefore inflicting this beating."
The elder said: "If you had taken my jewels, that would not be called theft; yet since they are now missing, it was not stolen by another. These jewels are currently back in my house."
Why is this? Because those who enjoy celestial blessings are the ones for whom such things may be used.
If Your Highness has any other desires, I shall provide them all to you; I have nothing with which to be parsimonious.
At that time, Prince Ajātaśatru conceived a thought of doubt:
"I have not yet sought anything from this elder; rather, after my father, King Bimbisāra, has passed away, I shall then seek his wealth, treasures, and various possessions."
Having formed this thought, Prince Ajātaśatru and Devadatta conspired together to take the life of his father, the King.
Eventually, after he had killed his father, he performed the consecration (*abhiṣeka*) himself and ascended the throne as king. He then summoned the householder Āloka and said to him:
"Householder, you shall be my elder brother; I wish to go and dwell together with you in your home. Whatever you may require, you should provide for me."
At that time, the householder Prabhāsa thought to himself:

"King Bimbisāra rules the world with the True Dharma, yet this man is fierce and evil, moreover rebellious; he killed his father the king and usurped the throne for himself by self-consecration. Now, before my very eyes, he utters words of deceit."
"If he wishes to stay in my house, I ought to comply; if I were to oppose him, my family would surely be ruined because of this man.
Having thought thus, he said: "Great King!"
"I know your mind; you must have some specific desire. I invite you to come to my residence, and whatever you may require, please enjoy it as you wish; I shall return to the royal palace later."
King Ajātaśatru said, "If you can do so,
it would be most excellent. Having reached this agreement,
the Great King first went to the householder's residence, and the householder in turn returned to the royal palace.
Whatever auspicious and superior signs the householder possessed, as well as his treasures and all his belongings, followed him wherever he went.
While King Ajātaśatru was in the householder’s residence, he saw the precious treasury appear seven times and vanish seven times. He thought to himself:
"The treasures and all the goods in this house will surely follow him away; I shall not be able to obtain them."

"I should now devise a separate and different stratagem: I shall secretly dispatch several extremely wicked men, all riding in a single carriage, to go to the house of the Elder Prabhāsa to steal his precious treasures."
When that man arrived, he devised a clever scheme and waited for an opportunity to commit a theft.
At that time, the elder Prabhāsa was atop a high tower, surrounded by his female attendants.
At that time, the female attendants saw the person carried in the carriage; they had already secretly recognized him as a wicked man who had come to commit theft.
Having seen him, the attendants laughed and pointed, saying, "This is the wicked thief."
At that time, the elder suddenly heard a voice laughing and saying, "I am fully aware of this matter.
Thereupon, the people kept it secret throughout the night; when morning came, many people saw it together and all cried out these words:
"King Ajātaśatru is a person of wicked rebellion; having murdered his father, the King, he has now dispatched these evil men to the house of the elder to steal precious treasures."
At that time, King Ajātaśatru, having learned of this matter, immediately dispatched a messenger to the house of the elder Prabhāsa, saying: "Elder!..."
"Why do so many people slander me?
At that time, having understood the king's intention, the Elder Prabhāsa immediately and swiftly drove away the wicked men.
The Elder then reflected to himself:
“King Ajātaśatru has committed a most heinous crime by murdering his father, the King; will he not do the same to me in the future?

To prevent such a calamity from occurring, I shall now renounce all that I possess. Recalling the Buddha’s prior prediction, I shall leave the household life to study the Path within the Buddha-dharma, sever all afflictions, and realize arhatship.”
"I should now go forth into homelessness under the Buddha.
Having reflected thus, he immediately brought forth his treasure store and performed various acts of compassion, benefit, and joy, such as giving alms.
The Sutra Spoken by the Buddha on the Causes and Conditions of Prince Prabhāsa, Scroll Three.
The Sutra Spoken by the Buddha on the Causes and Conditions of Prince Prabhāsa, Scroll Four.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master of the Western Heaven, the Imperial Attendant (Chao Feng Da) [Dānapāla].

Translated by the Imperial Preceptor and Dharma Master Shi Hu, recipient of the purple robe and Acting Minister of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices, by imperial decree: At that time, after the Elder Prabhāsa had performed various acts of compassion, benefit, and giving, he departed for the Buddha’s dwelling in secret, without informing his kinsmen or loved ones.
Having arrived, he prostrated with his head at the feet of the World-Honored One and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
May the Buddha now bestow upon me wholesome benefit. I now wish to go forth within the Buddha’s Dharma, receive full ordination, become a bhikṣu, and purely cultivate the holy life."
"May the Buddha, out of great compassion, accept me.
The Buddha said, "Welcome to my Dharma; diligently cultivate the holy life."

As he spoke these words, the hair and beard of the householder Āloka fell away of their own accord, and the saṃghāṭī robe naturally appeared upon his body, so that he took on the appearance of a bhikṣu.

Thereafter, carrying his alms bowl and pure water flask, for seven days and nights he dwelt with his mind fixed in right mindfulness, purely cultivating the holy life, his deportment worthy of emulation.
As if he were one who had observed a hundred years of seniority,
the Buddha took his own saṃghāṭī robe and covered the head of the bhikṣu Prabhāsa, whose faculties were tranquil and who dwelt with single-minded concentration.
At that time, a voice from the air proclaimed in praise:
"The Buddha now fulfills your heart's desire.

The bhikṣu Prabhāsa immediately aroused a mind of diligent effort and firm resolve, and he clearly observed the five destinies, the cycle of birth and death, revolving and turning in endless succession.

The various conditioned activities (*saṃskāra*) of sentient beings differ in many ways, causing them to fall into the cycle of birth and death; only the True Dharma of the Buddha can bring about their liberation.

Having contemplated in this manner, he perceived the Dharma of the Four Noble Truths, fully understood birth and death, and became detached from the notion of craving within the triple world. Regarding gold and jewels as equal to mud and soil, he severed all afflictions (*kleśa*) and realized the fruit of Arhatship.

He was fully endowed with the three types of supernormal knowledge and the six supernatural powers; he was supreme and peerless. Treading upon the void, he rose high, possessing mastery over his will. He remained entirely unattached to worldly matters such as fame and gain; thus, Śakra, Brahmā, and all the devas came to make offerings to him.
At that time, the assembly of bhikṣus, having witnessed this event, conceived doubts in their minds and addressed the Buddha together, saying:
"World-Honored One!
For what cause and condition does this bhikṣu Prabhāsa, while not yet ordained, manifest among human beings and receive such supreme blessings of the devas?"
"Having entered into the Buddha-dharma and just begun his life as a renunciant, he was able to sever all afflictions and realize arhatship?
The Buddha said, "O bhikṣus!"

This Bhikṣu Prabhāsa has long planted roots of merit which have now reached maturity; he has attained his benefit and, as it is determined according to what is appropriate, now is precisely the right time.
Therefore, Bhikṣu Prabhāsa, by virtue of the causal conditions of past wholesome deeds, has obtained such a fruit.

"Furthermore, Bhikṣus, you should know that the retribution of all karmas is produced from their own causes; it is not formed by the external element of earth, nor is it formed by the elements of water, fire, or wind, nor is it formed by any other aggregates, bases, or elements. Whether wholesome or unwholesome, all results of retribution are obtained solely through one's own karma."
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses for the bhikṣus:
"What all sentient beings have done, Even after passing through a hundred kalpas, it is not forgotten.
When causes and conditions converge at once, The retribution shall be experienced accordingly."
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
“Listen attentively, all of you, to the past causes and conditions of the bhikṣu Āloka.

Ninety-one kalpas ago, a Buddha appeared in the world named Vipaśyin Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidhyācaraṇasaṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān.”
That Buddha, together with a community of six million two hundred thousand bhikṣus, traveled to the great capital city of Pāṇḍumatī and stayed in one place.

That country had a king named Pāṇḍuma; he was of upright faith and ruled the kingdom according to the True Dharma. The land was vast and the population was flourishing; it was peaceful, prosperous, and joyful, free from all calamities such as disease and famine. There were no fears of strife, enmity, harm, or thieves, and the people were harmonious and endowed with auspicious qualities.

“At that time, in that city, there was an elder named Dravya-samudgata who possessed right faith in the Dharma. His family was immensely wealthy, with immeasurable treasures and riches, no different from those of the Heavenly King Vaiśravaṇa.”
At that time, when the householder learned that Vipaśyin Tathāgata and the assembly of bhikṣus had arrived in the city, he thought to himself:
"I wish to invite the Buddha and the assembly of bhikṣus to provide them with food and drink, and to have them dwell in my residence for the three months of the rainy season retreat."
Having reflected thus, he went to where that Buddha was.
Upon arrival, he prostrated with his head at the Buddha’s feet and withdrew to sit to one side.
Then, Vipaśyin Buddha, for the sake of the elder, proclaimed the essentials of the Dharma as was appropriate, instructing, exhorting, benefiting, and gladdening him.
Having heard the true Dharma, the Elder Dravya-seṇi rose from his seat, adjusted his robes, joined his palms toward the Buddha, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!..."

"I now invite the Buddha and the assembly of bhikṣus to my residence to partake of food and drink as offerings, and to observe the three-month rains retreat in my home. I shall provide and attend to all their needs; I pray that the Buddha, out of compassion, will accept my invitation."
Vipaśyin Buddha remained silent at once.

Seeing the Buddha’s silence, the elder Dravya knew that his invitation had been accepted; his heart was filled with joy, and he prostrated himself at the Buddha’s feet, then departed from the assembly and returned to his own home.

At that time, King Bandhumat heard that Vipaśyin Buddha, together with a community of six million two hundred thousand bhikṣus, was traveling and had arrived within this city. He immediately thought to himself:

"I shall now invite the Buddha and the community of bhikṣus to my palace to provide them with food and drink, and to remain there for the three-month rains retreat; I will supply them with everything they require as it is needed."
Having formed this thought, he immediately set out for the place where the Buddha was, surrounded by his ministers and attendants.
Upon arrival, he prostrated with his head at the Buddha’s feet and withdrew to sit to one side.
At that time, that Buddha, according to what was appropriate for him, expounded the essentials of the Dharma, instructing, benefiting, and gladdening him.
Having heard the Dharma, the king rose from his seat, adjusted his robes, joined his palms toward the Buddha, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!..."

"I now invite the Buddha and the assembly of bhikṣus to my palace to partake of food and drink as offerings, and to observe the three-month rains retreat within my palace. I shall provide all necessities—food, drink, clothing, bedding, and medicine—as required; I will serve and honor you with these offerings. I pray that the Buddha, out of compassion, will accept my invitation."
The Buddha said, "Great King!
I have already previously accepted the invitation of the householder Dravya."
The King said, "I pray that the Buddha will first come to my palace to accept the offerings of food; I shall then issue a command to the householder Dhanika. The Buddha said:
"Great King! It is the natural law that one must not violate a prior invitation.

At that time, King Bandhumat bowed his head at the feet of Vipaśyin Buddha; having paid homage, he departed from the assembly and returned to his palace. He immediately dispatched a messenger to the house of the householder Dhanika, delivering this command: [text continues]
"You should know this now: I have already invited Vipaśyin Buddha and the assembly of bhikṣus; you may prepare the offerings on another day.
The Elder Sañjaya said to the messenger, "I pray that Your Majesty will look upon me with compassion, for I have already invited that Buddha and the assembly of bhikṣus."
The messenger returned and reported this to the king. The king sent word again to the elder:
"Since you now reside within my kingdom, according to principle, it should be I who first provide for the Buddha."
The elder said to the messenger,
"If Your Majesty says that because I dwell within the kingdom, it is right for the King to be invited first, this is not actually the case;
I pray that Your Majesty will not obstruct me now."
The messenger returned and reported this in full. The King sent word again to the elder:
"You should know that even if you were to invite me, I would not obstruct you; however, if you can prepare a most excellent meal, the Buddha will come in person."
At that time, having heard these words, the householder Dravya immediately during that night kindled fragrant wood and prepared various kinds of pure, most excellent, and superior food and drink.
King Mandhātṛ likewise prepared food and drink within his palace.
When morning arrived, the householder arranged and adorned excellent seats and pure water vessels within his residence; having completed these preparations, he sent a messenger to the Buddha to say:
"The meal is ready and the time for eating has come. We pray that the Buddha will deign to visit us; now is the very hour."

At that time, Vipaśyin Buddha, together with the assembly of bhikṣus, dressed in his robes at the hour of eating, took up his alms bowl, and went to the house of the elder Sañjaya to receive his offerings.
Having arrived at that residence, the Buddha first washed his feet and took his place upon the most excellent and sublime seat;
the assembly of bhikṣus likewise each washed their feet and sat down in order.
The elder Dravya, with palms joined in reverence, stepped forward and prostrated at the feet of the Buddha.
Having paid his respects, he personally presented the most excellent food and drink to the World-Honored One, and then successively offered them to each of the bhikṣus.
At that time, after that Buddha and the assembly of bhikṣus had finished their meal, they set aside their bowls, washed their hands, and sat down in order.
The elder Dravya also sat respectfully before the Buddha, listening to the Buddha’s teaching of the Dharma.
"At that time, Vipaśyin Buddha, for the sake of the householder Sañjaya, preached the essential points of the Dharma as was appropriate, instructing, exhorting, benefiting, and gladdening him.

Having heard the Dharma, the householder was filled with great joy; he prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and after the householder Sañjaya had thus made his offerings, the Buddha departed from his house."
At that time, King Pūrṇabhadra, while still preparing food and drink within his palace and seeking to surpass the Elder, addressed his attendants, saying:
"The retinue of my consorts and ladies in this palace is vast; who among you can skillfully prepare such superior and exquisite food and drink as to surpass that of the Elder Saṃpadi?"
The attendant minister said:
"Your Majesty need only prohibit those who sell firewood; that elder himself will not be able to provide the meal for the Buddha."
The king acted according to his words and immediately issued a prohibition:
"If anyone persists in selling [firewood], they shall not remain within my kingdom.
At that time, when the householder Dravya heard the royal decree forbidding the sale of firewood, anger arose in his heart, and he spoke these words:
"Now, within my own house there is fragrant wood; why must I use that fuel to cremate my body?
At that time, the elder first lit fragrant wood and used fragrant oil within his house to prepare food and drink, and the fragrance permeated the entire great city.
When King Māndhātṛ had smelled this fragrance, he asked his attendants,
"From where does this exquisite fragrance come?
The attendants replied:
"This is the fragrance remaining from the incense wood used by the householder Dravya-seṭṭhi to prepare food and drink; it has come here.

When the king heard these words, he knew that the Buddha had already accepted the householder's invitation. He became even more distressed and said to his attendants, "Why is there no incense wood in my palace now?"
The attendant minister replied:
"There are no fragrant woods in the market; how could they be obtained?

Your Majesty should know that although the house of that wealthy elder is immensely rich, he has no offspring. Once he passes away, there will certainly be no successor, and all his possessions will revert to the King."
At that time, although King Pūrṇamāsa heard these words, he was still not pleased. A minister addressed the king, saying: "Great King!
Cease your grief for now. Your Majesty should invite the Buddha on another day to provide him with offerings; as you desire, I am able to make everything surpass that of the elder."

When the ministers and attendants had finished speaking these words, they immediately caused all gravel, impurities, and such things to be removed from the city of Pāṇḍumatinagara. They sprinkled it with sandalwood-scented water to make it pure, arranged rows of clean water jars, burned various exquisite incenses, and hung interlacing strings of genuine pearls. They erected banners and streamers and scattered various kinds of flowers, so that it was no different from the Garden of Joy in the heavens; it was pure, magnificent, and fully endowed with all manner of jewels.
They then prepared various seats made of exquisite gems.

The preparations were vast, consisting of various superior flavors—delicate, soft, sweet, and pure foods, complete in color and fragrance—like the celestial *sudhā*, a most pleasing and sublime flavor; such was the food that should be offered to the Honored One of the Three Realms.
Once the arrangements were completed, the ministers and attendants all addressed the king, saying:

"Now this great city, both inside and out, is pure and adorned with every variety of splendor; exquisite foods and drinks have all been prepared. We pray that Your Majesty will invite the Buddha to partake of a meal as an offering."
When King Bandhumat saw this, joy arose in his heart. He immediately dispatched a messenger to the presence of Vipaśyin Buddha and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"The meal is prepared and the time for eating has arrived; we pray that the Buddha will deign to come, for now is the very hour."

At that time, Vipaśyin Buddha, together with the assembly of bhikṣus, dressed in his robes at the hour of eating, took up his alms bowl, and went to the palace of King Māndhātṛ to receive his offerings.
Having arrived, the Buddha first washed his feet and took his place upon the most excellent and sublime seat; the assembly of bhikṣus likewise each washed their feet and sat down in order.

Then King Mandhātṛ took the precious auspicious vase and personally distributed pure water, starting from the Buddha and proceeding throughout; through the Buddha’s supernatural power, an auspicious dragon spontaneously stayed in the air, holding a hundred parasols to shade the head of the Buddha, the World-Honored One, and the bhikṣus.

The King’s principal consort stood by the Buddha’s side, holding a superb jeweled fan adorned with pearls, gold, and various precious gems; the other palace ladies likewise stood by the side of the bhikṣus, each holding a jeweled fan.
Then King Mandhātṛ approached and prostrated at the Buddha’s feet.
Having finished his prostration, he personally presented the finest food and drink to the World-Honored One, and thereafter offered them individually to each of the bhikṣus.

At that time, the householder Dhanika, knowing that the Buddha had also accepted King Pūrṇamada’s invitation, immediately dispatched a person to go secretly to the royal palace to observe how the arrangements for the decorations, food, and drink were being prepared.
When this man arrived there, he beheld all its extraordinary splendor; overcome with desire, he stopped and did not return. In this manner, others were sent repeatedly, yet none returned.
Finally, the elder himself went; having reached the royal palace, he observed the elaborate arrangements for the decorations and offerings, and then reflected to himself:
"I do not know who could have prepared such a display within the royal palace?"
"Why is it that in my own house there is no one capable of this?
Having had this thought, he returned to his own residence and said to the keeper of the treasury:

"You should take various gold and jewels and place them at the entrance of the gate. Should anyone come seeking them, you must give them as they wish; do not bring them inside, for I cannot see them."
At that time, having had this thought, the Elder Saṃpadaka entered his house, sat quietly in one place, and leaned on his staff, feeling displeased.
Then, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, seeing this with his pure divine eye, had this thought:

"In this world-system, the Elder Saṃpadaka is making offerings and giving alms to Vipaśyin Buddha; he is the foremost patron. His mind is pure in faith, and I should manifest my form to assist him in the construction."
Having formed this thought, he concealed his body as Śakra, Lord of the Devas, and manifested the appearance of a brahmin, proceeding to the residence of the householder Dhanika.
Upon arriving at that house, he said to the gatekeeper:
"You may enter and inform the householder, saying:"
"A Kausika clan Brahmin is currently outside the gate, wishing to see the householder.
The gatekeeper replied, "The householder has said:"
"Whoever comes here should not be admitted; if they have any request, it shall be granted according to their wish.
You, O Brahmin! If you have anything you desire, you should take it with you yourself; why must you seek an audience with the householder?"
The brahmin said: "I have no desire to take anything at all; I merely wish to see the elder now, so you should enter and announce me to him quickly."
Then the gatekeeper entered and reported, saying:
"There is a brahmin of the Kauśika clan standing outside the gate now, wishing to see the elder."
The elder said: "You may say to that brahmin:
'If you have something you seek, you should simply take it with you; why must you wish to see me?'"
Then the gatekeeper came out and reported this.
The brahmin spoke again:
"I have no request; I merely wish to see that householder."
Then the gatekeeper spoke again to the elder.
Thereupon, the elder granted him permission to meet.
Once the brahmin had entered, he addressed the elder, saying:
"Why are you now propping up your chin and appearing displeased?
What sorrow or anxiety do you have?
At that time, the elder spoke these verses:
“I do not speak of matters that cause sorrow; even if I were to speak of them, one could not be liberated from them.
If I am to bring about your liberation, I shall indeed speak for you.”
Then the brahmin said, "Simply tell me the cause of your sorrow, and I shall certainly resolve the matter for you. At that time,
after the householder Sañjaya had fully explained the cause, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, immediately withdrew his appearance as a brahmin, restored his own true form, and spoke to the householder:
"I am Śakra, Lord of the Devas; I shall now dispatch the devaputra Viśvakarman to assist you in preparing superior food and drink as an offering to the Buddha."
Having spoken these words, he vanished back into his celestial palace and immediately commanded the devaputra Viśvakarman, saying:
"Would it not be well if you were to go to the house of the elder Dravya and secretly assist in the preparations for the offerings to the Buddha?"

Then that devaputra, obeying the command of Śakra, secretly assisted the elder. By means of his supernatural power, he immediately transformed the great city, making it entirely pure like a celestial realm;
he arranged various exquisite and precious ornaments, and provided all manner of celestial thrones and sublime food and drink in full abundance.
The Nāga King Rāvaṇa spontaneously took his place in the air, holding a white parasol over the Buddha’s head, while the other auspicious nāgas each held parasols to shade the heads of the bhikṣus.
A celestial maiden stood by the Buddha’s side, holding a supreme jewel-fan adorned with gold; the other celestial maidens each held jewel-fans and attended beside the bhikṣus.
Then the householder Dravyaṇi took various kinds of food and drink of the finest quality and personally presented them to the Buddha and the bhikṣus.
At that time, King Pūrṇamāsa said to his messenger:
"You should go secretly to the house of the householder Dravyaṇi and observe the arrangements and the prepared food and drink; what is the state of affairs there?"
The messenger, having received his orders, immediately went there in secret and beheld all the extraordinary and magnificent sights; having seen them, he forgot to return.
The king again dispatched a close minister, who likewise did not return; he then sent the crown prince, who also failed to return.
Finally, the king himself went there and stood in concealment by the side of the gate.
At that time, Vipaśyin Buddha, knowing the king was outside, addressed the householder, saying:
"In the past, you committed an unwholesome verbal karma because of King Māndhātṛ; this constitutes a transgression.
That king is now at your house gate; you should go out quickly to repent for and apologize for your fault."
The elder immediately went out; having seen the king, he repented and reproached himself, then welcomed the king and led him inside.

Once the king had entered the house, he beheld all manner of exquisite celestial ornaments, food, drink, and so forth. Having seen these, he completely forgot his previous grievances and said to the elder:
"The offerings you present to the Buddha are as supreme as this; if you could continue to provide such offerings to the Buddha and the bhikṣus every day, they would be beyond compare."
Then, the householder Dravya, having aroused a pure mind, came forward and prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, making this aspiration:

“By means of these roots of virtue produced through giving such as they truly are to the Buddha and the bhikṣus, may I, upon being born in the future, obtain great wealth and mastery, with everything fully complete.”

In whatever place they are born, may they receive celestial blessings even while manifest as human beings; may they not give rise to excessive greed, but be fully endowed with conduct free from greed.
May they, as on this day, obtain the benefits of the wholesome Dharma, encounter the Buddha’s True Dharma, and take refuge in the Buddha by leaving the household life.
Having made this vow, Vipaśyin Buddha and the assembly of bhikṣus immediately stayed at the householder’s residence for the three-month rains retreat.
At that time, Śākyamuni Buddha addressed the bhikṣus, saying: "What do you think?"
At that time, during the Dharma of Vipaśyin Buddha, was the householder Dravya anyone else?
He is none other than the present bhikṣu Prabhāsa.

Because he uttered unwholesome words toward King Māndhātṛ at that time, the karmic retribution for this cause has not been lost; for five hundred lifetimes, he was burned by fire together with his mother, and even in this present life, it is likewise so.
However, because he previously planted roots of goodness and made great vows under the Buddha Vipaśyin, they have now reached maturity; he has become a wealthy elder, fully endowed with everything.

Manifesting among humans, he enjoyed superior celestial blessings; his performed deeds of merit and benefit, as well as his majestic power and other such matters, were no different from those during the time of Vipaśyin Buddha.
Now, at the very end, within my Dharma, he has left the household life to study the Path, severed all afflictions, and realized arhatship.

"O Bhikṣus! By this cause and condition, you should know that for all sentient beings, if they commit a single cause of black karma, they will certainly receive a single retribution of black karma; [and likewise for white karma]."
If one creates the cause of a single white karma, one will certainly experience the retribution of that single white karma.

Therefore, O Bhikṣus! Whether it be the cause of black karma or the cause of white karma, each and every fruit of retribution is certain and unfailing; you should know that all are produced by one's own actions.
"You monks, you should train yourselves in this way.
When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, the assembly of monks, having heard what the Buddha taught, were all greatly delighted; they accepted it with faith and practiced accordingly.
The Sūtra on the Causes and Conditions of the Youth Prabhāsa, Spoken by the Buddha, Scroll Four.
